INTERP-Q only has a weak 1-2alpha marginal guarantee, substantially below the stated target for common alpha values.

The experimental comparisons are too narrow for a top-tier acceptance. The paper does not compare against rank-calibrated class-conditional CP, APS/RAPS/SAPS-style scores, logit-adjusted or balanced-softmax long-tail models, or stronger long-tail training/calibration baselines beyond a focal-loss appendix.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially statements such as PAS being Pareto optimal in practice and INTERP-Q maintaining marginal coverage close to 1-alpha. These are empirical observations over selected methods and datasets, not general guarantees.

Evaluation of class-conditional metrics on the full long-tailed test sets is statistically fragile for rare classes with few examples. The truncated analyses help, but the main headline numbers still rely heavily on noisy per-class coverage estimates.

INTERP-Q requires choosing tau, but the paper offers no principled valid selection method. The discussion notes that choosing tau by calibration-set average size can violate exchangeability, which weakens practical deployment.

The simulated human decision-maker analysis is quite idealized and does not provide strong evidence for actual human utility or effort; the user-facing motivation is therefore only partially supported.
Reproducibility is weakened by the apparent missing code URL in the main text despite the claim that reproduction code is available.
